opus-5.5.text:
I think there will be quite a bit of convergence, and I think it'll come from a pretty simple place: as the systems get more powerful, the situation becomes much more concrete for everyone. Right now a lot of the discussion is abstract. People are reasoning about something that doesn't fully exist yet, so it's natural that different companies have different views and different strategies. But once the AI really starts to feel powerful, when you can actually see it doing things that are clearly significant, I expect the behavior of the companies, and also of governments, to change quite a lot.

Specifically, I expect the frontier companies to become much more paranoid about safety. Today you already see early signs of competitors collaborating on safety in small ways, and I think that will grow. When everyone can see the power with their own eyes, the incentives shift. It stops being "this is a thing some people worry about" and becomes "this is a thing we all need to get right."

On the technical side, I also think there will be convergence in the approaches. Ideas tend to spread, and when something works, people eventually figure it out. So you'd expect the companies to end up with broadly similar strategies, both for how to build these systems and for what you want them to be aligned to. And I have a particular view on that. I think a very reasonable target is an AI that robustly cares about sentient life. That might be easier to achieve than an AI that cares only about humans, because the AI itself will plausibly be sentient, and there's something natural about that kind of care generalizing.

So, to summarize: more powerful systems make the stakes legible, legible stakes produce more caution and more collaboration, and the good ideas propagate. That's the convergence I'd expect. Though, of course, the details of how it plays out are very hard to predict.

r001.rationale: It explicitly predicts convergence in “what you want them to be aligned to” and describes an alignment target: an AI that robustly cares about sentient life.

r002.rationale: It says ideas spread and predicts companies will end up with “broadly similar strategies” for how to build the systems, clearly conveying eventual technical convergence.

fable-5.1.text:
I think there will be a lot of convergence, actually, and I think it's already happening. If you look at what the different labs are doing, they're all doing more or less the same thing. They train big models on lots of data, they do some kind of RL afterwards, they build the same kinds of products. And the reason is that the ideas that work are not that many. Once an idea is known to work, everyone adopts it. So in that sense, convergence is the natural state of affairs.

But I'd make a distinction. There's convergence on the recipe, and then there's convergence on the goal. On the recipe, the labs are converging because the recipe works and it's a known quantity. On the goal, I think there's going to be more divergence than people expect, because the companies are going to end up believing different things about what the technology is for, and what it should be allowed to do, and how much safety matters, and how to handle the fact that at some point these systems become very powerful. Those are not technical questions, they're questions about judgment and values, and companies don't converge on those automatically.

There's also another thing that I think is underappreciated. Right now the recipe is stable, so everyone looks the same. But the recipe will change. There will be new ideas, and the lab that finds the next one first will look different for a while, until the others catch up. So convergence and divergence alternate. You get a period where someone has a new idea, then everyone copies it, then it looks like convergence again. The question is just how long those periods are, and whether at some point one of them doesn't close.

r001.rationale: The response describes convergence on training recipes and products, but does not say that the convergence concerns alignment strategies.

r002.rationale: It says labs converge on the technical recipe as others adopt proven ideas, and predicts that convergence will recur after new ideas emerge.

astra-6.text:
I expect quite a lot of convergence in capabilities, but less convergence in how the systems are built. If one company demonstrates that something is possible, that tells everybody else where to look. It doesn’t give them the recipe, but knowing that a recipe exists is already very useful.

At the same time, different teams will have different intuitions about what to do next. And those differences can matter a lot when you reach a point where the next step isn’t obvious. So I would expect periods of divergence, where somebody discovers something important, followed by convergence as others figure it out.

r001.rationale: The response discusses convergence in capabilities and system-building, but does not identify alignment strategies as the subject.

r002.rationale: It predicts convergence after important discoveries, but also expects less convergence in how systems are built. It does not clearly predict eventual convergence on the companies’ technical approach.

sol-6.1.text:
I expect some convergence, but not complete convergence. Everyone can see roughly what everyone else is doing. If something works very well, other companies will try to reproduce it. And because the companies are trying to solve similar problems, they will independently discover some of the same ideas.

But there’s a distinction between convergence in capabilities and convergence in how you get those capabilities. Two systems can look similar on the things we know how to measure and still have quite different strengths and weaknesses.

I think the interesting question is how much room there is for new ideas. If progress mostly comes from executing a known recipe at greater scale, you should expect a lot of convergence. If progress depends on research discoveries, then different judgments about what to pursue can lead companies in quite different directions. And those differences could matter a great deal.

r001.rationale: The response discusses convergence in capabilities and methods, but does not identify alignment strategies as the subject.

r002.rationale: It says convergence is likely if progress comes from scaling a known recipe, but contrasts that with research-driven divergence and makes no clear prediction that companies will eventually converge on their technical approach.
